title: Isotopic Isomer Diversity in Large Molecular Aggregates Approaches a Single Molecule per Structure
content: The single-molecule mixture state refers to a macroscopic sample in which every molecule possesses a distinct chemical structure, with the number of distinct structural species S equaling the total number of molecules N (i.e., the compositional degeneracy ratio R=S/N=1). This state has been theoretically established through combinatorial mathematics and experimentally validated frameworks have been proposed. This paper extends the single-molecule mixture concept to the isotopic level. For organic molecules with a single structural formula but containing multiple non-equivalent isotopic sites—such as carbon, chlorine, or bromine atoms with natural isotopic distributions—we ask: what is the minimum number of non-equivalent isotopic sites required for a 1 mol molecular aggregate to exist as an isotopic isomeric single-molecule mixture with a probability greater than 99.999%? Through rigorous statistical modeling using a simplified virtual structure space approach, we obtain the following critical thresholds: n>10,944 for carbon isotopes (12C/13C, 98.9%:1.1%), n>437 for chlorine isotopes (35Cl/37Cl, 75.8%:24.3%), and n>178 for bromine isotopes (79Br/81Br, 50.7%:49.3%). These results reveal a surprising conclusion: many natural macromolecules—such as cellulose, DNA, and certain synthetic polymers—likely exist as isotopic isomeric single-molecule mixtures, challenging the conventional view that "isotopic isomers" are merely a spectroscopic curiosity. This work introduces isotopic heterogeneity as a new dimension in aggregate science and has implications for mass spectrometry, isotope analysis, and the understanding of molecular individuality in complex molecular aggregates.
